content: Haverhill fever, also known as a form of rat-bite fever, is caused by the gram-negative rod bacterium Streptobacillus moniliformis. Symptoms typically manifest between two to ten days following a rat bite injury. The clinical presentation of the illness closely resembles that of a severe influenza-like syndrome. Patients often experience a moderate fever ranging from 101 to 104°F, accompanied by chills, joint pain (arthralgia), and a diffuse red rash. This rash is most commonly observed on the hands and feet. The causative organism, Streptobacillus moniliformis, can be identified through blood culture. Penicillin is the treatment of choice and is highly effective in managing the infection. In most cases, the body is capable of clearing the infection on its own, but antibiotic therapy significantly accelerates recovery and reduces the risk of complications. Complications are rare but can include serious conditions such as endocarditis (infection of the heart valves) and meningitis (infection of the protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord). This form of rat-bite fever is also referred to by alternative names, including Haverhill Fever and epidemic arthritic erythema.
